title: Performative Busyness
author: Chris Martin
summary: Chris Martin reflects on Cal Newport's 'Slow Productivity' and its central insight that 'pseudo-productivity' -- appearing busy as a proxy for doing good work -- has dominated knowledge work culture for decades. As remote and hybrid work expanded, visible activity (email replies, chat messages, desk presence) became the default signal of productivity because output was hard to measure. Martin argues that managers who demand busyness rather than results are often covering their own lack of clarity about what their teams should produce. Results-focused management requires more of managers -- it demands they define expectations clearly, communicate actively, and trust teams. The AI era risks creating a new layer of performative productivity: impressive-looking tool usage that doesn't actually improve outputs, and adoption driven by fear of replacement rather than genuine productivity gains.
points: * Newport's 'visible-activity heuristic' describes how, once knowledge work dominated, appearing busy replaced producing results as the primary productivity signal. * Managers who demand busyness are often doing so to cover their own lack of clarity about what their teams should be producing. * Results-focused management requires more of managers: clear outcome definitions, active communication, and genuine trust -- not just monitoring activity. * The AI era risks creating new forms of performative productivity -- impressive AI tool usage that signals effort without improving quality. * Newport's prescription: more trust, defined outcomes, and permission for knowledge workers to 'take a walk' rather than perform constant activity.
quotes: If you can see me in my office -- or if I'm remote, see my email replies and chat messages arriving regularly -- then, at the very least, you know I'm doing something.
Long work sessions that don't immediately produce obvious contrails of effort became a source of anxiety.
We need to be much more interested in results than we are in activity.
Lazy managers struggle with people who don't appear busy because their team's busyness is the only way they can know work is getting done.
It requires managers to have a firm understanding of what they want their teams to produce.
Wherever we go next, it is going to be important for us to consider that busyness and 'productivity' are not always related.
Sometimes the most productive thing you can do is go for a walk.
